summary:
Cosmic Lost & Found is an interactive web explorer for the hardware NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars, on Earth and in deep space, made for students aged 10 to 14. Players see the solar system from above, with Earth, Mars and the Moon at their approximate positions for the day, then pick a world and open the story of each of 17 items, from Apollo 11 and Viking 1 to Opportunity and Voyager 1. Every card says what the item is, what it discovered, where it is today and its “last signal”, the final contact from the mission.

It answers the challenge by turning abandoned hardware into stories, and the science it made possible, that children can explore on their own. It matters because these machines carry decades of discovery that few young people hear about. The app is built to be explored visually, by keyboard, by audio, in Libras and in a calm mode, in English and Portuguese. Facts come from NASA sources, and we state our limits openly: approximate scale, data still being checked, and AI-assisted code and text.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The app loads a JSON file of 17 NASA-related items and shows them in a 3D scene built with Three.js. The hub is a top-down map of the solar system, with Earth, Mars and the Moon placed at their approximate positions for today’s date, computed from simplified orbital elements from JPL. Students pick Earth, the Moon, Mars or “Toward the stars”, and a globe zooms to the spot where each item sits. A card then tells the story: what it is, what it discovered, where it is today, why it stayed and its last signal. Everything on screen is also real HTML, so it works with keyboard, touch and screen readers.

What benefits does it have?
Students get a short, story-based way into space history, with plain language for ages 10 to 14 and a mission-by-mission “last signal” that makes each item personal. Teachers get a free, open dataset with a source link on every item. Learners with different needs can choose high contrast, larger text, read-aloud, Libras (Brazilian Sign Language) via VLibras, or a calm mode with no motion or glow. It runs in a normal browser, with no install and no account.

What is the intended impact of the project?
We want more young people to know that NASA hardware is still out there, and to see the science it made possible, not only the missions that get headlines. We also want to show that an educational tool can be designed to be explored in several ways from the start. The dataset is open, so teachers or other teams can add items.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?
Tools:
- HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework.
- Three.js r160 for the 3D hub, globes and low-poly models.
- Web Speech API for read-aloud.
- VLibras (Brazilian government) for Libras.
- Lexend font, hosted locally.
- Python script to validate the data (structure, word limits, relations).
- Data and images: NASA sources (NSSDCA, science.nasa.gov, mars.nasa.gov, NASA Image and Video Library) and JPL orbital elements.
- Textures: three.js examples and Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0).
- AI assistants, Claude and Grok, for code and text drafts, recorded in AI_USAGE.md.
- Hardware: ordinary laptops and phones, tested in Chrome on desktop and mobile.

How is your project creative?

It frames abandoned hardware as lost-and-found objects with a personal ending, the “last signal”, instead of a spec sheet. The solar system uses real positions for the day, so the map changes from one visit to the next. Each item has its own low-poly 3D model standing on the globe, and the deep-space portal is a slowly rotating spiral. The same interface also has a calm mode and a no-WebGL fallback, so the design is not tied to one way of experiencing it.

What factors did your team consider?
- Audience: ages 10 to 14, so we set an 80-word limit per card and plain wording.
- Accessibility: we aimed for WCAG 2.2 AA and built the keyboard, audio, Libras and calm paths from the start. No one with a disability has tested it yet, and we say so.
- Honesty: the scale is fictional and shown with a fixed notice, positions are approximate, and every item has a source. Fact-checking against the sources is still in progress.
- Performance: it should run on school Chromebooks and weaker phones, so we capped the canvas resolution and avoided heavy effects, though we have not measured frame rate.
- Scope: two days of development, so we cut features such as a live Voyager distance and offline mode and listed them as next steps.
- Responsible AI use: we kept a log of what AI did and what the team decided or checked.
